title: A matrix is where it sends the basis vectors: determinant, morph, rotation angles and singular values
summary: Four Math Studio views of linear maps. In 2D the columns of a matrix are arrows and the determinant is the signed area of the image of the unit square; in 3D, a rotation parametrized by Euler angles loses a degree of freedom at pitch 90 degrees (gimbal lock), and the singular value decomposition splits any matrix into rotate, stretch, rotate.

media.alt: Screenshot of the Transform workspace. A skewed grid of blue lines covers the plane, an orange arrow and a blue arrow from the origin mark the images of the unit vectors, and a thin orange parallelogram shows the image of the unit square. A readout at upper right gives the matrix 2, 1.5; 2, 1, determinant minus 1.000000, the area of the unit square's image minus 1 and the statement orientation flipped, F is mirrored.

read_the_figure.question: What does this matrix do to the plane (stretch, shear, flip), how much does it scale area, and does it keep orientation?
read_the_figure.axes: 2D transform: x and y in the plane, the grid is the image of the integer grid; amber arrow is A applied to the first basis vector, sky-blue arrow to the second; the shaded parallelogram is the image of the unit square. 3D views: orientation of a body drawn with three rings (angles) or a sphere mapped to an ellipsoid.
look_at: The two arrows are the columns of A. Read them off: (2, 2) and (1.5, 1). The parallelogram they span has signed area ad - bc.
The determinant line: -1 here, so area is preserved in magnitude but orientation is flipped; the readout says 'F is mirrored'. The inverse has determinant 1/det = -1.

Morph (last screenshot): M(t) = (1 - t) I + t A for A = diag(2, 0.5); at t = 0.56 the readout shows the determinant of what is shown as 1.123457 equal to the area of the image: a continuous interpolation whose determinant is not constant.
Gimbal lock (second screenshot): three nested rings are the three Euler angles; at pitch 90 degrees two rings align, so two angles control the same rotation.
SVD (third screenshot): the unit sphere is mapped to an ellipsoid, whose axes are the singular values in directions given by the singular vectors; a unit cube is shown in the same frame.
read_the_figure.proves: Everything about a linear map in the plane is in the columns: determinant for area and orientation, the grid for shear and stretch. The 3D views show two facts about rotations: three angles can collapse to two, and a matrix is a rotation, a stretch and a rotation.
if_wrong: Determinant zero: the map collapses the plane to a line and has no inverse.
Determinant negative: orientation flipped; a reflection is hiding in the matrix.
A rotation described by Euler angles near pitch 90 degrees: numerical derivatives of angles blow up.
Reading singular values as eigenvalues: they coincide only for symmetric positive matrices.
must_check: That the matrix is printed and the columns identified with arrows.
That the determinant and orientation statement are present.
That the angle convention (order of rotations) is stated for 3D.
That the SVD view shows both singular vectors and singular values.

terms.meaning: A map that sends sums to sums and scales to scales; fully described by a matrix.
The signed factor by which the map scales area (volume) in 2D (3D).
Three successive rotations about coordinate axes used to describe an orientation.
The loss of one rotational degree of freedom when two Euler axes line up.
Factorization into rotation, diagonal stretch and rotation.

remember: The first column of A is where the first basis vector goes.
Area scales by |det A|; the sign says whether orientation is kept.
(1 - t) I + t A is a straight-line morph; its determinant changes along the way.
At pitch 90 degrees the rotation depends only on a combination of the other two angles.
Singular values are the lengths of the semi-axes of the image of the unit sphere.

steps.title: Determinant of the screenshot matrix
steps.note: The area of the image of the unit square is 1 and its orientation is reversed: the F of the picture is mirrored.

steps.title: The morph and its determinant
steps.note: At t = 0.5556 this is 1.5556 times 0.7222 = 1.1235, the value printed (1.123457). The determinant of the endpoints is 1, but along the path it is not.

steps.title: Why Euler angles lose a degree of freedom
steps.note: Two different pairs of angles with the same difference give the same orientation: the map from angles to rotations is no longer locally one-to-one.

steps.title: SVD of a shear
steps.note: The unit circle becomes an ellipse with semi-axes 1.618 and 0.618; their product is the area scale, which is 1 for a shear.

worked.problem: Find the singular values of [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and check their product.

analyze.q: What changes about the grid when the determinant goes from 1 to -1?
At t = 0 of the morph the determinant is 1. At t = 1 it is 1. Why is it 1.12 in between?
Explain how two Euler angles can describe the same rotation at pitch 90 degrees.

evaluate.q: A game uses Euler angles for a camera and the camera jerks when the player looks straight up. Diagnose and propose a fix.
Is a straight-line morph between two rotation matrices a rotation at each t? Why or why not?

create: Choose a matrix with determinant 0 and predict what the grid and the parallelogram look like.
Write down a matrix whose SVD has singular values 3 and 1/3 and sketch the ellipse.

checks.q: What do the columns of a matrix represent?
checks.answer: Where the basis vectors go; the first column is the image of the first one.

checks.q: Why is the area of the unit square's image the determinant in absolute value?
checks.answer: The image is the parallelogram spanned by the columns; its area is |ad - bc|.

checks.q: Does a determinant of 1 mean the map is a rotation?
checks.answer: No: a shear has determinant 1 and is not a rotation. A rotation also preserves lengths and angles.

checks.q: Design an animation that makes gimbal lock obvious.
checks.hint: Show the rotation changing with angles.
checks.answer: Animate two of the angles around the lock position and show that the body spins about the same axis for both.
